Income by age is a snapshot of different people, not a forecast of your career

Four interactive graphics compare conditional means and medians, age-band population counts and income-recipient shares from an official Canadian snapshot.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Fixed public snapshot released 29 April 2026, reviewed 25 October 2026. Canada; Total - Gender; Employment income. The year control selects observed 2022–2024 cross-sections and never forecasts. All income amounts are annual 2024 constant CAD, with zero incomes excluded from the published means and medians. Income is not take-home pay or a full-time-worker salary quote. Counts and conditional income measures have different denominators. Quality letters are retained from the source: A Excellent, B Very good, C Good, D Acceptable. They are not confidence intervals, and no comparison is declared statistically significant. Different age bands contain different people; no individual career path, causal age effect or future pay increase is estimated.

The central idea

Before using an age-group income figure in a plan, check who is included. A recipient median, a whole age-band count and an individual’s future income answer different questions.

01

Ask which people sit behind the income number

A headline about what people earn at thirty or fifty can seem useful for a long-term plan. The first task is to identify the population and the income measure before inserting a figure into a household spreadsheet.

This article selects Canada, Total - Gender and Employment income from Statistics Canada’s Table 11-10-0239-01. Six disjoint age bands cover ages fifteen and older. The overlapping 25–54 aggregate and the overall 15+ row are excluded from the charts.

The mean and median explicitly exclude zero incomes. Their population therefore differs from everyone in an age band. The table also provides a number of persons and a number with income, allowing the figures to be read beside their denominator.

For the 2024 reference year, the 25–34 band has an estimated 6,081,900 persons and 5,313,300 with employment income. Its recipient median is CAD 49,400, compared with a mean of CAD 56,900. The conditional median cannot be assigned to every person in that age band.

02

Keep employment income separate from take-home pay and a job quotation

Statistics Canada’s employment-income classification includes paid-employment income and net self-employment income. It is broader than a single employer’s annual salary quotation. The selected series is not after-tax cash.

A small employment-income amount in an older age band also does not describe the group’s entire retirement income. Pension and other income sources are outside this selection. These graphics do not measure total resources, poverty or retirement adequacy.

Someone can have employment income for only part of the reference year. These charts do not select full-time, full-year workers, identify hours worked or calculate an hourly wage. Dividing a published annual median by a standard number of working hours would not turn it into a verified wage rate.

All monetary observations here use 2024 constant dollars, including the earlier years selectable in the control. This price basis supports comparison within the snapshot. It does not make a 2022 amount a nominal payment received in 2024, and it does not update any observation into today’s prices.

A household budget needs its own net receipts, payment dates and commitments. An actual offer or self-employment forecast also needs its own hours, costs and deductions. Treat the statistics as context for questions to investigate, rather than an available source of cash.

03

Read the amounts and the recipient share together

The first chart places the mean and median on the same zero-based dollar axis within each age band. The difference between them is informative about those two summaries, but it does not reveal the entire income distribution or a particular person’s position in it.

The count chart supplies a second view. Each complete bar is the estimated age-band population. The first segment is the source count with employment income; the remainder is calculated by subtraction. The full population and the recipient count must not be added as though they were separate groups.

The third chart divides the recipient count by the population count for the same age and year. For ages 25–34 in 2024, that calculation is approximately 87.36%. It describes income reporting over the reference year. It is not a Labour Force Survey employment rate or a forecast probability that a reader will find work.

The scatter chart combines that share with the conditional median, one point per age band. The axes keep both questions visible: how much does the midpoint recipient report, and what proportion of the age group reports the selected income? No connecting line turns the ordered age labels into one person’s history.

04

Retain the quality letters without inventing confidence intervals

The table supplies quality codes, and the figures retain them beside the relevant age labels. A means Excellent, B means Very good, C means Good and D means Acceptable. In the amount chart, the two letters refer to the mean and median respectively. In the count chart, they refer to the recipient count and the full age-band count.

The 2024 income mean and median for ages 65+ carry B, while the two count inputs carry A. A ratio calculated from those counts does not automatically inherit a new published quality grade. The graphics label the ratio as a derived calculation.

The Canadian Income Survey’s 2024 release explains that estimates have sampling variability. No confidence limits for these comparisons are supplied here, so the charts do not claim that a difference between age groups or years is statistically significant.

The control switches among observed 2022–2024 snapshots. It recalculates count ratios and moves the quality labels with their source values. It neither forecasts a later year nor removes uncertainty by displaying another decimal place.

05

Build a personal earnings scenario from personal evidence

The age bands contain different people at one point in time. A higher median in a later band does not establish what a person in an earlier band will earn ten years later. Differences in work participation, hours, occupations and the people represented would require separate evidence before any cause could be assigned.

For a personal plan, start with current receipts and document a small set of explicit scenarios: unchanged income, a confirmed change in hours or a separately justified career transition. Keep hypothetical pay growth visibly distinct from the observed national data. Include periods when income may fall or stop, alongside the spending and accessible cash that must carry them.

Finally, keep the snapshot’s version. The 2024 release revised earlier estimates, so mixing values copied from different releases can manufacture an apparent change. Recheck the current table before reusing a figure, retain the reference year and price basis, and avoid treating a statistical midpoint as a guaranteed personal outcome.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. The graphics use 72 curated observations from Statistics Canada Table 11-10-0239-01, released 29 April 2026. Select an observed reference year from 2022 to 2024. Means and medians exclude zeros; monetary values retain the source’s 2024 constant-dollar basis. Count complements and ratios are labelled as derived calculations. No personal earnings projection is made. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Statistics Canada · Table 11-10-0239-01 and full-table CSV ↗

    Released 29 April 2026; full CSV and metadata downloaded and verified 25 October 2026. Seventy-two observations select Canada, Total - Gender, Employment income, six disjoint ages and four statistics for 2022–2024. Quality letters are preserved. Count differences and ratios are separately calculated. Income units are 2024 constant CAD, excluding zeros; counts use units. The metadata identifies earlier methodology and population revisions.

  2. Statistics Canada · Classification of income sources: employment income ↗

    Official classification reviewed 25 October 2026 for the distinction between employment income and a salary-only quotation. No tax or hourly-wage calculation is applied to the statistical amounts.

  3. Statistics Canada · Canadian Income Survey, 2024 ↗

    Release dated 29 April 2026, reviewed 25 October 2026 for sampling variability and revision context. No confidence interval or causal effect is inferred for an age-group comparison.
